heading: Collecting water
body: Swales, berm, dams, rainwater tanks and greywater — make water move slowly, spread out and enter the ground, every drop.

heading: Learning outcomes
body: Explain that a level swale following a contour line can reduce the speed of running water and spread it so that it is absorbed in a suitable place.
Explain why dams need a designed overflow route and a site assessment.
Explain what a first-flush diverter does and why tank water still needs to be checked for safety.
Keep greywater away from people, food and drinking-water pipes.

heading: Two ways of swale design
body: A level swale following a contour line is one design way of reducing the speed of running water. Its channel follows a level contour line so that the water spreads and is absorbed into suitable ground.

Other swales are made on purpose to have a small slope, together with a safe designed exit place. Soil, slope, water outflow and movement of storm water determine which way is suitable. Ask a trained local advisor to assess the site before digging.

heading: A swale can let water soak in
body: This picture shows a level swale following a contour line as an idea. Water may spread along the side of the channel and soak in where the soil allows.
It does not show how deep moisture reaches in your soil. Look at the soil, slope and overflow route before building.

heading: Berm below
body: The soil taken out makes a berm on the downhill side. It is a place where trees can be planted when the site design is suitable.
Trees may use moisture kept in the nearby soil after rain; the result differs by place.

heading: Storms need a safe overflow route
body: Heavy rain may fill a swale faster than the water soaks into the ground. Plan a safe overflow route before digging.
The route must not damage the slope or send damaging water to a neighbour. The swale or dam below must be able to receive it safely.
Ask a trained local advisor to assess the soil, slope and storm-water flow. The picture is not a construction design.

heading: Check the overflow route before digging
body: A swale needs a planned overflow route in heavy rain. Check it before digging.
Water may go to another swale or a dam only if the site assessment shows that the route, exit place and receiving place can carry the water flow without damage.

heading: Look at the site before digging
body: The slope alone does not tell you whether a swale is suitable or not. Soil, water outflow, unstable ground and water from above the slope all matter.
Keep the soil well covered. Seek local assessment before digging in very steep, wet or unstable ground. Grass barriers and soil steps (terraces) also need design that suits the place.

heading: Look: roots help hold the soil
body: Roots help hold the soil along a planted contour line.
Choose a way of controlling erosion with local advice; very steep ground needs a site assessment.

heading: Keep rain of the dry season
body: A dam or pond can keep running water, but the amount available depends on local rain, catchment, water loss and how much water you use.
Rain seasons differ throughout South Africa. Use local records and plan for dry periods; there is no promise that a dam will stay full.
Before changing a watercourse or building water-storage works, check the required permission from the water authority.

heading: Design the overflow before the wall
body: A dam needs site investigation and a design made by a person properly trained for it. Water running in the catchment, soil, foundations, risk downstream and the safe overflow route (spillway) all matter.
Don't think annual rainfall tells you the size of the flood or how much water will be stored.
Uncontrolled overflow can wash away and break the wall. Plan a safe route for excess water before building.

heading: Dam and overflow: idea
body: Design the overflow before the wall — a wall that water goes over can break very badly.
Water running in the catchment is only one of the things needed. A person properly trained for it must assess the site and the design of the dam and overflow before building.

heading: Look after the dam and its banks
body: Water can be lost through evaporation and seepage into the ground. Check the water level and look for seepage or erosion.
Keep the overflow unblocked and keep the covering of the banks as set out in the design. Do not plant trees on the earth dam wall.
Animals can damage the banks and add dung to the water. Their presence does not make the water clean or safe.

heading: Your roof is a place for collecting water
body: Your roof can collect rainwater. The amount depends on the size of the roof, rain and loss.
Check whether roof materials are suitable for collecting rainwater before connecting a tank.
Use the roof size as seen from above together with local rain records. Then consider water that does not enter the roof channel (gutter), is diverted or overflows from a full tank.
The amount of annual rain does not tell you how much water there will be in dry time. Compare the water you have with planned use.

heading: Divert the first dirty water
body: Water from the roof can carry dust, dung and other dirt. A first-flush diverter (device that diverts the first water) keeps part of the first water from entering the tank.
The amount of water that must be diverted depends on the roof and the system. Use the vendor's instructions for size and maintenance; there is no single volume that suits every roof.
The diverter does not make the remaining water safe to drink.

heading: First water to the tank: idea
body: The first-flush diverter keeps the first water from the roof from entering the tank.
Size it and maintain it to suit your roof; the following water still needs to be checked for safety.

heading: Match tank size and water demand
body: Tank size depends on water demand, rain, roof size and length of dry periods.
Record the use you plan and estimate your need using your records. Compare that with the water you have in the seasons.
Plan what you will do when the stored water decreases. The name of the province itself cannot tell you the size of tank you need.

heading: Keep stored water safe
body: Keep the tank covered, cover openings with a screen to prevent insects, and maintain the roof, gutter and diverter. Keep rainwater separate from drinking-water pipes.
Water that looks clean may have germs or chemicals. Ask the local health authority about testing and suitable cleaning for the intended use.
A basic filter alone is not a guarantee of drinking water. Water used on food plants also needs safety testing.

heading: Used water differs by source
body: Used household water may contain germs, salt, cleaning products and other things. The guidelines do not describe each source in the same way.

South African guidelines differ about kitchen water and laundry water. Do not include toilet water, nappy water, washing of a sick person or washing of animals in the plan to reuse it. Do not reuse water with dangerous chemicals.

heading: Get local advice before reuse
body: Before reusing, ask the municipality and a trained local sanitation advisor to assess the exact source, the household's water and sanitation services, the intended use and the place.
If this advice is not available or not clear, do not reuse the water. Soil and mulch do not kill viruses in dirty water.

heading: The picture is not a farm design
body: This general picture is not a farm design that has been checked or approved. It does not show that the source, route or destination is safe.
Check with trained local advisors before reuse. Soil and mulch do not kill viruses in dirty water.

heading: Prevent contact and pollution
body: Prevent contact with people or animals. Do not join wash water to drinking-water pipes, spray it, let it stand, or let it leave the property to the street, drain or stream.
If a water-reuse system is already working and the water smells very bad, stands, or harms plants, stop using it and seek the advice of a trained local advisor.

heading: Field work
body: Build an A-frame level with three poles and a string tied to a heavy object.
Use it to find one level line across your slope.
Take a photo of the A-frame and the line you marked.

heading: Check your work
body: My A-frame is built and I tested it.
Turn it around — it must read the same way.
I marked at least three points at one level across my slope.
The line I marked crosses the slope, it does not go down along it.
Minimum possible time for real work: 5 days.
